root_draft.speaker: agent
root_draft.text: TheRot is a cold fungal cathedral whose generosity draws a colony into a living, hungry network. Its towering caps, biological light and milky ground make a place to live; the mat helps heat shelter, while the Sheen, fast decay and still-living harvest change how the colony works. Its best medicines demand a guarded expedition and fresh brewing. Symbionts offer real benefits with lasting bodily costs, and animal kin share wounds or mend in company. The hwelgrue makes the same bargain enormous: it returns metal, takes the fallen alive, and carries a ship core whose living log rewards patience while its extraction rewards a difficult fight. The vat, purge draught and earned mat root let the colony carry particular lessons away; teas and symbionts keep their existing limits. These connected promises need separate demonstrations, then a colony scene showing that comfort, danger and belonging feel like one place. The free mod stands on its own fungal cast; shared engines and campaign additions keep their own responsibilities.

failure_modes: F1: It is a collection of fungal bonuses and punishments, not the generous hungry cathedral he chose: comfort never matters, joining is an obvious upgrade, or carried rewards have no satisfying use. Sources: design/RimMandrake/biome_experiences_2026-10-20.md; design/Jawa/worldbuilding/biomes/the_rot.md; OWNER:1792691344764566303.

F2: Its hunger feels like a trick: a prize is undefended despite the promise, wounds look like unrelated attacks, faint knocking gives no usable rescue, or the core's loss was unreadable. Sources: design/Jawa/worldbuilding/biomes/the_rot.md; ITEM:ROT_HEALTH_SHARING_1; ITEM:ROT_STILL_ALIVE_SWALLOW_1; OWNER:1790963785567080878.

F3: Living there becomes chores, waiting or unsafe state: a large colony cannot manage the ecology, the log asks only idle time, or settings/reloads/failed output placement lose bodies, rewards or honest behavior. Sources: src/RimMandrake/TheRot/Source/RM_GutMother.cs; src/RimMandrake/TheRot/Source/RM_NavigatorLog.cs; src/RimMandrake/TheRot/Source/RM_TheRotMod.cs.

asks.title: What makes the generosity dangerous
asks.picture: Written thought experiment, not a capture: a cold colony builds on warm mat, wins a healing brew, and begins to rely on the place. Later the same forest sickens an exposed worker and takes a fallen companion into a giant.
asks.text: Which moment makes this feel like your Rot, and where does the proposed root misunderstand that feeling?
asks.why: F1. A pile of useful fungi and separate punishments could obey the feature list while missing the generous, hungry place in your chosen sentence.
asks.guess: The comfort should be sincerely useful, so accepting its bargains feels tempting; the danger should feel like the same living ecology. I would lead with that connection.
asks.tree_change: If home and reliance lead, centre the root and colony interaction scene on living with the network. If the expedition and its price lead, centre those while retaining the built home and giant branches. His correction rewrites dependent promises. Without a reply the root remains unapproved.
asks.decision: Root emphasis and what an otherwise functional Rot can still get wrong.

asks.title: The first demonstration
asks.picture: Written scene drafts: A, a cold working colony on living mat, protecting stores and tending a shared-wound herd; B, a guarded trip to brew a scarce medicine before it dies; C, knocking and a ship ping from the hwelgrue, a rescue, then a choice about its core; D, a later cold landing using the earned mat root.
asks.text: Which scene should come first when you judge whether the Rot understands you, and what failure there would make you stop?
asks.why: F1/F2. The four older draft bars do not record a flagship pick, and one busy scene could hide independent failures.
asks.guess: B first: it joins beauty, help and hunger in one trip. I would follow with a separate giant scene and a cold-stop reward scene.
asks.tree_change: A makes routine colony life the flagship; B makes the grove expedition first; C makes the giant dilemma first; D makes the carried reward first. The other capabilities retain scenes. Only an explicit pick later binds showcase 1; root approval alone does not.
asks.decision: Flagship selection and its rejection case, without putting other built features up for removal.

asks.title: A normal day with forty colonists
asks.picture: Written thought experiment: a settled forty-person colony has roofed stores, a freezer full of living produce, mat-floored rooms and workers crossing the forest. The player has learned the ordinary precautions; no special crisis is running.
asks.text: What should still occupy the player each day, and what should a well-arranged base have made easy?
asks.why: F1/F3. Heat, decay and exposure can make a distinctive routine, or become constant small chores. The existing clocks do not settle the acceptable daily burden.
asks.guess: Good shelter and storage should solve routine losses; harvest heat and exposed work should still influence planning. I would test a competent base, not only an unprepared landing.
asks.tree_change: If sound planning mostly solves daily hazards, require a stable-base control and put remaining pressure on expeditions. If active tending remains central, name the recurring job and prove it stays readable at forty colonists. Warmth and rot rules remain; only provisional rates and interaction checks follow his picture.
asks.decision: Routine work and colony-scale acceptance, rather than new machinery.

asks.title: The moment a grove answers
asks.picture: Written thought experiment: a prepared party approaches valuable caps. One side is dangerous with spores; touching a lure can call nearby defenders. Empty-forest alarms were already accepted, so this picture promises no guaranteed arriving creature.
asks.text: What should a careful player be able to notice and act on before the danger closes around the harvester?
asks.why: F2. Defended prizes are settled; the fair chance to read and answer that defense is not specified by a radius or a trap lookup.
asks.guess: The grove should reward a plan and leave a clear retreat choice, with surprise about the particular defender. I would reject an unexplained instant injury as the whole expedition.
asks.tree_change: If recognition before approach matters, add a recognition and preparation scene. If the disturbance is the warning, require a measurable chance to interrupt or rescue after it. If a sudden trap is acceptable, do not invent advance warning; demonstrate the consequence and recovery instead. Existing defense and accepted misfires stay.
asks.decision: Warning/action window and rejected cheap implementation; known wiring bugs are fixes, not owner decisions.

asks.title: When the herd bleeds
asks.picture: Written thought experiment: one tame gromma is shot; nearby agarikin acquire wounds too. A chittik beside them does not join that clique. Elsewhere, an injured durrok recovers faster among its own kin. The ruled clique table stays fixed.
asks.text: What should you see that makes sharing an injury understandable before you mistake the other wounds for a second attack?
asks.why: F1/F2. The table is already decided. The player still needs to distinguish a shared cost from unrelated damage and understand why gathering the herd helps.
asks.guess: A short visible connection at the hit, backed by a useful inspect line, should explain it without letters for every injury. I would judge this at normal play zoom with a real herd.
asks.tree_change: If the moment itself must explain it, add a brief readable-cue requirement and a no-link comparison. If selection is enough, use an inspect/health-panel scene and avoid a new transient cue. If no extra sign matters, add no cue leaf; still prove clique isolation and tamed participation.
asks.decision: Player-facing explanation of existing kin mechanics, not their already ruled membership.

asks.title: Finding someone late
asks.picture: Written thought experiment: after a battle, the player hears faint knocking from a hwelgrue and finds a companion with little time left. Fighters are injured and the rest of the colony is busy. The name and remaining hours are already in the inspect line.
asks.text: What rescue should still be possible at that late moment, and what would make a death feel earned rather than stolen?
asks.why: F2. Naming hours and offering release does not establish a useful rescue chance; a helper can report a pawn spawned outside while it is dead.
asks.guess: A prompt, committed response should have a real chance, with worse injuries for delay and an unmistakable final warning. I would judge both a fresh swallow and a deliberately late discovery.
asks.tree_change: A late rescue promise needs a scene with a defined travel/fight window and an explicitly living survivor. If late discovery may be hopeless, bind the readable deadline and a separate recoverable earlier case. If the answer turns on how faint knocking sounds, show an audible exploration before binding the cue.
asks.decision: Rescue opportunity, deadline fairness and sound acceptance; no re-asking whether swallowing exists.

asks.title: Living beside the treasure map
asks.picture: Written thought experiment: the ship receives another fragment of the dead log. The party can extract the core now, ending unread entries, or stay with a dangerous living giant to hear more. Current defaults mean a long wait for the complete log; campaign tiles still wait for final paint.
asks.text: What does the time between entries look like in the story you would enjoy playing: a temporary camp, repeated returns, or another pattern?
asks.why: F1/F3. The alive-versus-extract dilemma is already chosen. A timer can turn it into idle waiting unless the intended visit has enough useful play.
asks.guess: A temporary camp with useful excursions, and the option to return, fits the bargain. I would make a full itinerary earn its elapsed time rather than only force pings in a proof.
asks.tree_change: A camp needs an integrated stay with actual ping intervals and local risk. Repeated returns need persistence and real departure/landing continuity. A different itinerary changes provisional timing and the ordinary-use scene, while keeping core uniqueness, ship-gun damage and death ending unread entries.
asks.decision: Pacing and player itinerary; not the settled range reward or carrier rule.

asks.title: Choosing to remain joined
asks.picture: Written thought experiment: the clan is preparing to leave. Some people carry useful symbionts. Keeping one means keeping its bodily price; the draught removes it at the cost of sickness and possible organ injury. The religious rite remains deferred.
asks.text: What should the player understand before deciding who remains joined on the next journey?
asks.why: F1/F2. The bargains are settled, but benefits can be obvious while hunger, mental risk, sun intolerance or the purge cost arrive too late to choose knowingly.
asks.guess: Each host should make the benefit and the continuing cost easy to compare, and the draught should disclose what it takes away and what it can hurt. I would use one departure decision, not another tutorial system.
asks.tree_change: If an ordinary health/inspect view suffices, bind that information there. If committing to a purge needs a deliberate warning, add the specific confirmation/cost preview he names. If uncertainty is part of the story, state which consequences may be uncertain rather than inventing hidden costs. No rite or launch siege is revived.
asks.decision: Informed body/departure choice and readable irreversible costs.

asks.title: The cold stop after the reward
asks.picture: Written thought experiment: the clan earns the living mat root, installs it on the ship and later stops somewhere cold. It needs raw food there; fed roots can bud, and hungry mat stops warming and later retreats. The heat ceiling, raw-food diet and budding are already decided.
asks.text: At that stop, what difficulty should the mat have meaningfully eased, and what preparation should the clan still need?
asks.why: F1/F3. The existing promise that it helps without trivialising cold needs a player situation; a room-temperature increment alone does not say the reward was worth earning.
asks.guess: It should reduce the heating burden enough to make a cold stop attractive, while insulation, food and backup heat still matter. I would compare the same stop without it and with one and several roots.
asks.tree_change: If it primarily saves fuel, measure useful heating saved across that stop. If it enables emergency shelter, require a survivable preparation window and a hunger failure case. If it chiefly warms a travelling home, demonstrate actual ship/floor carry and repeated landings. Keep the settled cap and food/bud rules; tune only the experience numbers still provisional.
asks.decision: Concrete usefulness acceptance for the already ordered portable reward.
